q: How long does a radio message take between Earth and Mars?
explain: Light travels at 300,000 km/s, yet Mars sits 55 to 400 million km away. That's why rovers can't be driven with a live joystick—they follow commands sent in advance.

q: How high is the atmospheric pressure on the surface of Mars?
explain: Mars averages around 6 millibars compared to 1,013 on Earth. With so little pressure, liquid water quickly boils or freezes, so astronauts need pressurized suits.

q: What is almost all of the Martian atmosphere made of?
explain: About 95% is CO₂, with nearly 3% nitrogen, 2% argon, and only trace amounts of oxygen.

q: What did Perseverance's MOXIE experiment accomplish?
explain: MOXIE split oxygen from CO₂ by heating it to ~800 °C. Between 2021 and 2023 it produced 122 grams—proving crews can make air and rocket fuel on Mars.

q: Why did Perseverance land in Jezero Crater?
options: It is the hottest spot on Mars
Billions of years ago it held a lake and river delta
explain: Jezero held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago. Where water once flowed, ancient life could have existed and left clues preserved in delta rocks.

q: What did Perseverance find in the rock Cheyava Falls in 2024?
options: 'Leopard spots' that may be a biosignature of ancient life
explain: The spots show chemistry often linked to microbes on Earth. In 2025 NASA reported it as the clearest potential biosignature yet, pending study in Earth labs.

q: Why does Perseverance store samples inside sealed tubes?
options: So a future mission can bring them back to Earth
explain: Earth laboratories hold instruments far more sensitive than any rover payload. Hermetic seals protect the cores from contamination.

q: What ended the InSight mission in 2022?
explain: Settling Martian dust blocked sunlight on its solar arrays until power ran out. That's why cleaning our base solar panels matters!

q: What did InSight mainly study?
options: Marsquakes and the interior of Mars
explain: Its seismometer recorded over 1,300 marsquakes and helped scientists map Mars's crust, mantle, and core.

q: What helped Spirit and Opportunity last years longer than planned?
options: Wind gusts that cleared dust off their solar panels
explain: Lucky 'cleaning events' from wind restored their power. Opportunity operated for nearly 15 years despite a 90-day mission plan.

q: Why is radiation more hazardous on Mars than on Earth?
options: Mars is closer to the Sun
Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a very thin atmosphere
explain: Earth's magnetic shield and thick atmosphere deflect particles. On Mars, solar energetic particles and cosmic rays reach the surface almost directly.

q: According to Curiosity RAD, how intense is radiation on the Martian surface?
options: One day equals about 3 months of natural background radiation on Earth
A thousand times lower than Earth
explain: RAD measured ~0.64 millisieverts per day in Gale Crater, whereas Earth averages ~2.4 mSv per year. That's why your suit radiation only climbs day by day.

q: What did Curiosity measure during the May 2024 solar storm?
options: The largest radiation surge since landing in 2012
explain: An X12 flare hurled particles toward Mars, and RAD measured 8,100 micrograys—like 30 chest X-rays. An astronaut would have needed shelter immediately.

q: Can auroras happen on Mars?
options: Yes; MAVEN spotted planet-wide auroras in May 2024
explain: Incoming solar particles strike the upper atmosphere and glow. Without a global magnetic field, auroras on Mars can sweep across almost the entire planet.

q: When a solar storm arrives, what best protects an astronaut on Mars?
options: A bunker covered with meters of regolith or water
explain: Dense mass (regolith, water, plastic) absorbs energetic particles. That's why the base's shelter is built behind thick regolith walls.

q: What is NASA's DONKI?
options: A space weather database tracking flares, CMEs, and storms
explain: DONKI catalogs space weather events and how they connect. The solar alerts in this game come from real events in that database.

q: What is a CME (coronal mass ejection)?
options: A huge cloud of magnetized plasma launched by the Sun
explain: A CME can take one to several days to reach a planet—giving time to broadcast warnings and race to shelter.

q: What is the WSA-Enlil model used for?
options: Predicting where a CME travels and when it will arrive
explain: It simulates solar wind and CME trajectories. Sometimes forecasts update: an alert can turn into a near miss, just like in the game.

q: What are the perchlorates found in Martian soil?
explain: Phoenix detected them in 2008. Perchlorates can harm the thyroid, so dust tracked into a habitat must be cleaned carefully.

q: Why did Perseverance collect samples of regolith (dust and sand)?
options: To understand how dust affects astronauts and hardware
explain: Fine dust creeps into suits, seals, and filters and can harm lungs. Perseverance collected its first regolith samples in December 2022.

q: Which Perseverance instrument uses ultraviolet light to search for organic compounds?
explain: SHERLOC shines an ultraviolet laser on rock surfaces: organic compounds and certain minerals respond with a telltale optical 'fingerprint'.

q: What does PIXL measure?
options: Chemical elements inside a rock using X-rays
explain: PIXL fires X-rays onto tiny specks of rock and maps its chemical elements grain by grain.

q: What does SuperCam's laser do?
options: Vaporizes a pinpoint spot from meters away to analyze its glowing plasma
explain: From the flash's light and its infrared spectrometer, SuperCam identifies minerals—including ones that hold water.

q: Which weather station monitors the climate in Jezero?
explain: MEDA measures temperature, wind, pressure, humidity, dust, and UV radiation. Air in Jezero swings from ~−20 °C by day to near −80 °C at night.

q: How long is one Martian day (a 'sol')?
explain: A sol lasts about 24 hours 39 minutes. Mission teams sometimes live on 'Mars time', shifting their schedules later each day.

q: How long is a year on Mars?
explain: Mars orbits farther from the Sun and takes nearly two Earth years to complete one lap, so Martian seasons last almost twice as long.

q: If you weigh 50 kg on Earth, what would a scale read on Mars?
explain: Martian surface gravity is about 38% of Earth's—you could jump nearly three times higher!

q: Why does Mars look red?
options: Iron oxide (rust) in its surface dust
explain: Martian soil contains oxidized iron minerals. Winds loft that fine rust dust into the air, tinting even the sky.

q: What historic milestone did Ingenuity, the helicopter carried by Perseverance, achieve?
options: The first powered, controlled flight on another planet
explain: It first lifted off in April 2021. Designed for 5 flights, Ingenuity completed 72 before rotor damage retired it in 2024.

q: How does Earth listen to spacecraft at Mars?
options: With giant dish antennas of the Deep Space Network (DSN)
explain: The DSN operates sites in California, Spain, and Australia so at least one site always faces Mars as Earth rotates.

q: How do Mars rovers send most of their science data back to Earth?
options: Relayed through orbiters such as MRO overhead
explain: Orbiters carry larger antennas and pass overhead multiple times per sol, beaming back far more data.

q: Why does NASA enforce a career radiation limit for astronauts?
options: Because cumulative radiation raises lifetime cancer risk
explain: NASA sets a career limit of 600 millisieverts. That is why the radiation meter in this game never goes down—it accumulates.
